rationale: Mixed-methods empirical evaluation (n=1,209 household surveys, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions across five pilot sites in Kajiado County, Kenya) of the WaterStarters franchise model for drinking water access, measuring safe, affordable, and reliable household water outcomes. Criteria 1, 3, and 4 are clearly satisfied. Under the narrow Criterion 2 reading, the abstract plausibly implicates utility-ownership/franchise governance and tariff/cost-recovery/hybrid-financing rules affecting affordability and access, but could alternatively focus on NGO project delivery and commercial return; therefore full-text review is required (unsure).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Under literal/plain Criterion 2 wording, the study clearly includes an institutional and governance arrangement (a private/community franchise management and hybrid financing model) affecting household water access. Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, full-text inspection is required to determine whether the evaluation analyses specific tariff/cost-recovery/subsidy rules, contractual franchise terms, or utility-ownership/regulatory mechanisms governing access rather than generic NGO pilot project delivery and business financial viability.

evidence_quotes.quote: This innovative model sought to improve sustainable water access by empowering local private and community-based organizations to manage water systems through a hybrid financing approach.
Using a mixed-methods design, the study drew on survey data from n=1,209 households, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions across five pilot sites.

The findings indicated that the model improved access to safe, affordable, and reliable water, with notable benefits in hygiene, reduced disease incidence, and time savings for households, particularly benefiting women and girls.
